# Projects

## Health Risk Modeling Analysis

Investigated whether physical food access or socioeconomic factors better explain chronic health outcomes across Lancaster County, Nebraska. Found that educational attainment was a substantially stronger predictor of obesity than proximity to grocery stores. That result held across both linear and nonlinear models.

**Tools:** Python, pandas, scikit-learn, geopandas\
**Data:** ACS (U.S. Census Bureau), CDC PLACES, OpenStreetMap

[View Report (PDF)](files/Math_in_the_City___Group_4__Spring_2026.pdf){target="_blank"}

<details>

<summary>See technical details</summary>

- Engineered distance based and density features from OpenStreetMap using OSMnx (distance to nearest grocery store, fast food density per km²)
- Built a multiple linear regression model achieving R² ≈ 0.49. Compared against random forest (R² ≈ 0.59).
- Feature importance analysis confirmed percent without a high school diploma (importance 0.721) as the dominant predictor over physical food access (0.143)
- Performed 5 fold cross validation to evaluate model stability across tract subsets
- Visualized spatial clustering of obesity, poverty, and transit access across census tracts using geopandas

</details>

## Health Risk Modeling, Extended Analysis

After completing the class project, I wanted to test whether adding more policy relevant variables would change the findings. The original analysis identified educational attainment as the strongest predictor of obesity. Adding SNAP participation rates and age distribution data from the ACS shifted that picture considerably.

**Key finding.** SNAP participation rate (r = 0.81) emerged as the strongest single predictor of obesity, stronger than education, poverty rate, or any food access measure. SNAP is a program that can be targeted and expanded, making it a more actionable consideration than structural factors like education level.

**Tools:** Python, pandas, scikit-learn, geopandas, statsmodels\
**Data:** ACS 5-year 2023, CDC PLACES 2025, OpenStreetMap, TIGER/Line 2020

[View Notebook](files/analysis.html){target="_blank"}

<details>

<summary>See technical details</summary>

- Added SNAP participation rate, percent population under 18, and percent 65+ from ACS to the original feature set
- Random forest feature importance showed snap_rate (0.547), percent_no_hs (0.277), and pct_under_18 (0.062). Food access variables combined below 0.05.
- Linear regression R² = 0.574. Random Forest R² = 0.668 on the held out test set. Repeated K fold CV mean R² = 0.602 (RF) vs 0.389 (LR).
- Spatial mapping revealed SNAP concentration and obesity hotspots overlap almost perfectly in Lancaster County's urban core
- Decision tree (max depth 4) confirmed SNAP rate as the primary splitting variable
- The age split is notable. pct_65_plus negatively correlates with obesity (r = -0.46) but positively with coronary heart disease (r = 0.74), suggesting distinct drivers across outcomes.

</details>
